And we're going to drift into frame, cut into the interior of the spaceship. The air will fade into, or will drift over into Harper's profile coming in and locking the stars. We're going to do something kind of dramatic here. When we get to her floating, we don't want to see her body out because we want to bounce back out to see that she's floating. I wonder if we can do this. Maybe that we get tiresome as kind of a runner where we connect all the transitions with either a speed zoom or an actual camera movement to the next cut. That would probably be hard. Consistency would probably be tough. Maybe we can do that where we can do that in a few places though. Just be tiring to try and keep it up for the whole thing. Maybe for select scenes and cuts between the scenes we can do that.

blocking.imagePrompt:
Use case: identity-preserve
Asset type: 16:9 wide music-video starting frame for one continuous alien-coast experience.
Input 1: full-body Harper reference for adult auburn curls, freckles, gray short-sleeve T-shirt, gray trousers and bare feet; recreate her standing naturally instead of floating. Input 2: original detailed Harper interior portrait for face. Input 3: established alien planet for the world palette and jagged archipelago design.
New scene: Harper experiencing a virtual planetary shore as if physically there. Show the place directly and leave its VR nature unexplained: no digital overlay, headset, spacesuit, projected avatar transparency or spacecraft. A beautiful immense non-terrestrial coast of broad long peach/rose tidal flats, shallow luminous turquoise sea, dark blue angular rock spires/archipelagos and pale peach clouds in a cyan-violet hazy sky. Strong long curving tide bands leading into the distance. Camera is an oblique elevated wide view, Harper occupies left-of-center but is large and clearly identifiable, full adult body about half the image height, barefoot on damp reflective flats. Her proportions stay human, but she is about three times the scale of nearby alien plants and creatures, her interactive projection can be oversized in this world. Place readable small alien flora in foreground/around her feet: translucent violet ribbed fan fronds, amber stalks with segmented umbrella crowns, sparse low coral-like pale-blue colonies. A few distinctive tiny six-legged pearlescent shelled tidal animals move in shallow channels; avoid earthly crabs, gulls, fish, palms or trees. There is quiet natural diversity rather than clutter. Harper faces toward the sea in a three-quarter view with her face still readable, relaxed delighted/wondering expression, arms beginning to open but NOT fully stretched yet, shoulders low, two anatomically natural arms/hands and two bare feet clearly posed. Leave ample lateral room for the arms to open wide in the animation; hands not near image boundaries. Coastal camera sees out to open ocean and spires. Initial tide is midway across the flats; broad shallow parallel tide fronts will gently advance/recede in response to her gesture later. Do not show a frozen towering tsunami or destruction. Upper-right warm sunlight rim-lights auburn curls; turquoise/peach marine color reflected in gray fabric. Painterly cinematic graphic-novel finish exactly consistent with the references, tactile expressive illustration, no photography. No moons, ship, equipment, jewelry, text, labels or HUD.

storyboardProposals.sourceNoteText:
Chorus 1 / What is her mission?

User direction October 10: only chorus 1 and chorus 2. Chorus 1 begins around 43.5s on How much can you do with it all? Harper intends to positively influence worlds with nascent life and accelerate their progress; consequences remain ambiguous. Plan a general arc, not a cut per lyric. Explore jump-cut or zoom-out-blur entry, zoom blurs or fades within the chorus, and one-second handles each side. A/B ideas below are assistant proposals for discussion, not selected imagery.

A â€” Living-world invitation: zoom out from the coast tide into an immense shallow basin of nascent alien colonies; Harper is small at its edge, studying a stalled living pattern. Match the curved tide to the colony shape. Her attention conveys care before any intervention.

B â€” Worlds in her care: jump or zoom-out blur into an oblique view of Harper beside several enlarged living-world projections. Each contains a distinct simple ecosystem rather than an abstract planet icon. She studies their differences and chooses one; this reads as a mission with multiple destinations.

Cut/continuity: Entry alternatives: a decisive jump cut on the question, or a brief zoom-out blur linking tide/basin to world/projection. This proposes replacing the tail of space-011 from frame 1046; retain its accepted still and v11 until a branch is selected.

Branches may be mixed; these are imagery markers, not locked cuts. Reserve 24-frame lead-in and lead-out handles for new chorus footage.

The flow travels through the scene; first one organism opens, then its neighbors respond. Hold through Little something rather than cutting for both phrases.
storyboardProposals.sourceNoteText:
Do something / Little something: a modest intervention

User direction October 10: only chorus 1 and chorus 2. Chorus 1 begins around 43.5s on How much can you do with it all? Harper intends to positively influence worlds with nascent life and accelerate their progress; consequences remain ambiguous. Plan a general arc, not a cut per lyric. Explore jump-cut or zoom-out-blur entry, zoom blurs or fades within the chorus, and one-second handles each side. A/B ideas below are assistant proposals for discussion, not selected imagery.

A â€” Open a channel: one quiet gesture redirects a small trickle of water toward a dormant fan-frond colony. The flow travels through the scene; first one organism opens, then its neighbors respond. Hold through Little something rather than cutting for both phrases.

B â€” Offer a catalyst: she releases a tiny luminous seed-like instrument into a young alien habitat. Local creatures approach it and reorganize their activity in their own way. Keep the catalyst modest; its light becomes a transition anchor, not an explosion or instant advanced civilization.

Cut/continuity: Possible gentle dissolve between intention and response, or a short matched zoom blur toward the small intervention. A can continue the same world; B can follow either mission framing.

storyboardProposals.sourceNoteText:
Youâ€™re something / A right little something: agency and uncertainty

User direction October 10: only chorus 1 and chorus 2. Chorus 1 begins around 43.5s on How much can you do with it all? Harper intends to positively influence worlds with nascent life and accelerate their progress; consequences remain ambiguous. Plan a general arc, not a cut per lyric. Explore jump-cut or zoom-out-blur entry, zoom blurs or fades within the chorus, and one-second handles each side. A/B ideas below are assistant proposals for discussion, not selected imagery.

A â€” The world answers back: pull back from the opening colony to Harper, now dwarfed by spreading life. At one edge the new growth diverts water from another patch. She notices and pauses: hopeful response with an unresolved ecological cost, not a disaster reveal.

B â€” The result exceeds the plan: the catalyst starts a beautiful branching pattern; living inhabitants reroute it into something different from her intended design. A close reaction shows fascination and a trace of doubt. A right little something can refer to her, the catalyst, or the unpredictable living result.

Cut/continuity: Let the intervention develop across both phrases. Avoid separate literal illustrations for each something. Carry a light pulse or branching shape toward the orbit passage.

Branches may be mixed; these are imagery markers, not locked cuts. Reserve 24-frame lead-in and lead-out handles for new chorus footage.

SHOT: SIDE/FRONT three-quarter medium-wide sphere on RIGHT traveling toward distant warm-white star at LEFT, calm deceleration. Single aft drive ring on trailing RIGHT side, not on left. Harper clearly visible floating entirely INSIDE transparent hex-geodesic sphere, auburn hair, adult scale gray coverall, both feet contained. Sparse subtle light paths trail toward right. Ship occupies about half frame height, no enormous face or superimposition. Dark open space permits destination vista as separate subsequent cut.
REFERENCE ROLES: image1 accepted spacecraft design and Harper scale; image2 motion-light language only. Preserve exact sphere technical geometry, no added structure. Transparent sphere uses faint cyan HEXAGONAL facets. Physical adult Harper must remain inside the sphere.

Full-frame 16:9, no captions, lettering, watermarks, borders, panels or collage. Adult Harper has freckles, hazel-green eyes, short voluminous curly auburn hair, warm-gray long-sleeved survival coverall with closed collar, gray belt and graphite closed utility shoes, tiny unlettered amber arm tab. She floats weightlessly aboard the open sphere. Planet-side Harper is ONLY a translucent cyan holographic projection, never a physical visitor. Ship: transparent faint cyan geodesic sphere, ONE graphite OUTER equatorial band with amber lights, small upper/lower technical plates, entry port and ONE vertical aft engine ring; NO extra inner cockpit ring or conventional airplane cockpit. Planet: emerald continental forests, copper inland seas and ivory weather systems, cyan atmosphere. Community: original small intelligent nonhuman quadrupeds matching the creature reference, teal textured skin, ochre face/throat and paired fan crests, amber eyes, short blunt muzzle, dexterous forefeet and short balancing tail. Four limbs total, no humanoid bodies or Earth tribal costume. Woven seedpod dwellings, root paths, gardens and local tools. Include ONLY subjects explicitly required by the shot; reference objects must not leak into unrelated landscapes or cosmic views.

FINAL EXCLUSIONS: No creatures, no settlement, no station, no people outside the sphere, no superimposed faces, no montage, no duplicated ship, no extra inner equatorial ring. Do not include reference station. Only one ship with one outer equatorial band and one aft drive ring. Keep polar plates small and unobtrusive.
